# Objective

Optimize the condition number of the product $PQ$, where $P$ is the Cholesky
factor of the reduced-form error covariance matrix and $Q$ is an orthogonal
rotation, in order to recover well-conditioned structural shocks from a
reduced-form VAR. This document gathers the problem definition: the condition
number and its norms, the optimization problem over orthogonal matrices, the
implications for the forecast-error decomposition of "Criteria for SVAR model
selection: A proposal", and the supporting mathematical appendix.

# Condition number

Before proceeding to the next section, we will define the condition number of a
matrix and its interpretation in terms of numerical sensitivity and matrix
inversion. This concept is important for understanding the stability of
numerical computations involving matrices, particularly in the context of
solving linear systems and inverting matrices.

## Definition

The condition number of a nonsingular matrix measures the **sensitivity** of the solution of
a linear system **to perturbations** in the data. For a system $Ax=b$, a large condition number in
$A$ implies that small changes in $b$ may generate comparatively large changes
in the solution $x$, whereas a value close to one indicates that the system is
well conditioned. Importantly, conditioning is a property of the matrix itself
rather than of the numerical algorithm used to solve the system.

For any consistent matrix norm, the condition number is defined as

$$
\kappa_p(A)=\|A\|_p\|A^{-1}\|_p
$${#eq-conditionNumber}

with $\kappa_p(A)\geq 1$ for every nonsingular matrix, and $p$ denoting the matrix norm. If $A$
is singular, its condition number is effectively infinite, reflecting the
absence of a unique and numerically stable solution.



::: {.callout-important}

Consequently, matrices with condition numbers close to one are considered well
conditioned, while very large values indicate near-singularity and greater
numerical sensitivity when computing inverses or solving linear systems.

:::


Under the induced Euclidean norm ($\|\cdot\|_2$), the condition number can be expressed as

$$
\kappa_2(A)
=
\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)}
{\sigma_{\min}(A)},
$$

where $\sigma_{\max}(A)$ and $\sigma_{\min}(A)$ denote the largest and smallest singular values of $A$. Thus,
a matrix becomes increasingly ill conditioned as its smallest singular value
approaches zero. In the particular case of an **orthogonal** or unitary matrix, all
singular values are equal to one and therefore

$$
\kappa_2(A)=1.
$$

For more details about the condition number using the $\ell_2$-norm, see
@sec-singularValues.

## Definitions for different norms

The operator norm corresponding to the $p$-norm for vectors is:

$$
\|A\|_{p}
=
\max_{x\neq 0}
\frac{\|Ax\|_{p}}{\|x\|_{p}}.
$$

### Norm $\ell_{\infty}$:

$$
\|A\|_{\infty}
=
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|,
$$

which is simply the maximum absolute **row** sum of the matrix.

### Norm $\ell_{1}$:

In the cases $p=1$ the norm can be computed as:

$$
\|A\|_{1}
=
\max_{1\leq j\leq n}
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ij}|,
$$

which is simply the maximum absolute **column** sum of the matrix; see @sec-proofNorms
for proof of this result.




# Optimization problem involving orthogonal matrices

We now formally introduce the proposed approach for recovering structural shocks
through orthogonal rotations of the Cholesky factor of the reduced-form error
variance-covariance matrix.

The admissible set is defined as

$$
\mathcal{O}(K)
=
\left\{
Q\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}
:
Q'Q=QQ'=I
\right\}.
$$

Combining the reduced-form covariance decomposition, the unit-variance
normalization of the structural shocks, and the Cholesky identification, the key
equations are the following. The reduced-form innovations $e_t$ of the SVAR
satisfy

$$
e_t = B_0^{-1} w_t,
$$

with $w_t$ the vector of mutually independent structural shocks normalized to
have identity variance-covariance matrix, $\Sigma_w = I$. Therefore, the
reduced-form error covariance matrix is

$$
\Sigma_e
=
\mathbb{E}[e_t e_t']
=
B_0^{-1}\Sigma_w B_0^{-1'}
=
B_0^{-1}B_0^{-1'},
$$

and the benchmark recursive (Cholesky) identification sets $B_0^{-1}=P$, the
lower-triangular Cholesky factor of $\Sigma_e$. In general, any orthogonal
rotation $Q$ of $P$ delivers an equally valid factorization of $\Sigma_e$:

$$
\Sigma_e
=
B_0^{-1}B_0^{-1'}
=
PQQ'P'
$$

where $P$ is the Cholesky factor associated with the benchmark recursive
identification, and $Q\in\mathcal{O}(K)$ is an orthogonal rotation matrix.

Therefore, orthogonal rotations generate alternative structural decompositions
that preserve the reduced-form variance-covariance matrix. This provides the
basis for defining an optimization problem over $Q$ to select a structural
decomposition according to the criterion of minimizing the condition number of
$B_0^{-1}=PQ$.

The optimization problem can be formulated as follows:

$$
Q^{*}= \text{argmin}_{Q\in\mathcal{O}(K)} \kappa_{p}(PQ),
$${#eq-optimizationProblem}

where $p\in\{1,4,\infty\}$. The case $p=2$ is excluded because, under the Euclidean norm, $\kappa_2(PQ)=\kappa_2(P)$;
hence, the objective function does not depend on $Q$ (see @sec-singularValues).

::: {.callout-note}
For a complete exposition of the SVAR models and the standard notation
conventions used in the project ($B_0$, $B_1$, $\psi$, $w_t$, $e_t$,
$\Sigma_e$, and the Cholesky identification), see
`OSST/docs/OSST_standard_svar_notation/OSST_standard_svar_notation.qmd` and
`OSST/docs/svar_dogmatic_model/svar_dogmatic_model.qmd`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## In simple terms
The idea is to find the orthogonal matrix $Q$ that minimizes the condition
number of the product $B_0^{-1}=(PQ)$, which represents a rotated version of the Cholesky
factor $P$. By minimizing the condition number in $\ell_{\infty}$ norm, we aim to improve
the numerical stability of the resulting structural shocks and ensure that they
are well-conditioned for subsequent analysis in different samples.
:::

## Properties of orthogonal matrices {#sec-orthogonalMatrices}

An orthogonal matrix $Q$ is a real-valued square matrix whose columns and rows
are orthonormal vectors.

- **Orthogonality**: $Q'Q = QQ' = I.$

- **Inverse**: $Q^{-1} = Q'.$

- **Preservation of the Euclidean norm**: $\|Qx\|_2 = \|x\|_2.$

- **Preservation of inner products**: $(Qx)'(Qy) = x'y.$

- **Determinant**: $\det(Q) = \pm 1.$

- **Singular values**: $\sigma_i(Q) = 1, \qquad \forall i.$

- **Condition number under the 2-norm**: $\kappa_2(Q) = 1.$

- **Eigenvalues**: $\left|\lambda_i(Q)\right| = 1.$

- **Preservation of the identity matrix**: $QIQ' = I.$

- **Preservation of covariance under orthogonal rotations**: 

If

  $$
  \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)=I,
  $$

then

  $$
  \operatorname{Var}(Q\varepsilon)=I.
  $$


## Future Work: Numerical Optimization Methods

* Investigate numerical optimization methods suitable for solving the
  orthogonal-matrix optimization problem described above.

* Compare alternative approaches for enforcing the orthogonality constraint $Q'Q=I$,
  including:

  * optimization using Givens-angle parameterizations;
  * projected gradient methods;
  * Riemannian gradient descent on the orthogonal group $\mathcal{O}(K)$;
  * Riemannian trust-region methods.

* Investigate numerical approaches for handling the non-smooth nature of the
  infinity-norm condition number.


* Investigate the use of multiple initial orthogonal matrices (*multi-start
  optimization*) to reduce the risk of convergence to poor local minima.

* Compare the numerical methods in terms of:

  * convergence;
  * computational cost;
  * numerical stability;
  * preservation of the orthogonality constraint;
  * achieved value of $\kappa_\infty(PQ)$.

* Determine which numerical optimization method is most appropriate for the
  dimensions and restrictions considered in the project, and document the
  selected algorithm and convergence criteria.


## Singular values and $\ell_2$-norm {#sec-singularValues}

For a square matrix $A$, the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^HA$, where $A^H$
is the conjugate transpose, are called singular values of $A$. The singular
values are always non-negative and are usually denoted by $\sigma_i(A)$, where $i=1,\ldots,n$ for an
$n\times n$ matrix. The singular values can be ordered as follows:
$$
\sigma_i(A)= \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^HA)},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
$$

By the definition of the $\ell_2$-norm, we have that

$$
\sigma_i(PQ) = \sqrt{\lambda_i(Q^HP^HPQ)} = \sqrt{\lambda_i(P^HP)} = \sigma_i(P),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
$$

where the second equality follows from the property of preservation of inner
products of orthogonal matrices, see @sec-orthogonalMatrices. Therefore, we have
that

$$
\sigma_{\max}(PQ) = \sigma_{\max}(P),\qquad \sigma_{\min}(PQ) = \sigma_{\min}(P),
$$

and then looking for a $Q$ that minimizes the condition number of $PQ$ is
equivalent to minimizing the condition number of $P$, which is a constant. And
this is a trivial result, because the condition number of $P$ is a constant and
does not depend on $Q$.

## Proof of the result for the $\ell_\infty$-norm and $\ell_1$-norm matrices {#sec-proofNorms}

### $\ell_\infty$-norm

**Proof:**

Let

$$
\alpha
=
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|.
$$

We have that

$$
\forall x\in \mathbb{R}^n
\qquad
\|Ax\|_{\infty}
=
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j
\right|
\leq
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
|a_{ij}||x_j|
$$

$$
\leq
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
|a_{ij}|\|x\|_{\infty}
=
\|x\|_{\infty}
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|
=
\|x\|_{\infty}\alpha.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\|Ax\|_{\infty}}{\|x\|_{\infty}}
\leq
\alpha
\qquad
\forall x\in \mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}
\Rightarrow
\|A\|_{\infty}\leq\alpha.
$$

On the other hand, if we define

$$
k
=
\arg\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|
$$

If $\alpha=0$, then $A=0$ and the result follows immediately. Otherwise, define

$$
z=
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{sgn}(a_{k1})\\
\vdots\\
\operatorname{sgn}(a_{kn})
\end{pmatrix},
$$

we have that

$$
\|z\|_{\infty}=1
$$

and

$$
Az
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\operatorname{sgn}(a_{kj})a_{1j}
\\
\vdots
\\
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\operatorname{sgn}(a_{kj})a_{mj}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

so that

$$
(Az)_k
=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\operatorname{sgn}(a_{kj})a_{kj}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{kj}|
=
\alpha.
$$

Thus,

$$
\frac{\|Az\|_{\infty}}{\|z\|_{\infty}}
\geq
|(Az)_k|
=
\alpha
\Rightarrow
\|A\|_{\infty}\geq\alpha.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\|A\|_{\infty}
=
\alpha
=
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|
\qquad
\square
$$



### $\ell_1$-norm


**Proof:**

Let

$$
\alpha
=
\max_{1\leq j\leq n}
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ij}|.
$$

We have that

$$
\forall x\in \mathbb{R}^{n}
\qquad
\|Ax\|_{1}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j
\right|
\leq
\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
|a_{ij}||x_j|
$$

$$
=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\left(
|x_j|
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ij}|
\right)
\leq
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|x_j|\alpha
=
\alpha
\sum_{j=1}^{n}|x_j|
=
\alpha\|x\|_1
\Rightarrow
$$

$$
\Rightarrow
\frac{\|Ax\|_1}{\|x\|_1}
\leq
\alpha
\qquad
\forall x\in \mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}
\Rightarrow
\|A\|_1\leq\alpha.
$$

On the other hand, taking

$$
z=e_k,
$$

the $k$-th vector of the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, with

$$
k
=
\arg\max_{1\leq j\leq n}
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ij}|,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{\|Az\|_1}{\|z\|_1}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ik}|}{1}
\overset{\text{def }k}{=}
\alpha
\overset{\text{def. induced norm}}{\Rightarrow}
\|A\|_1\geq\alpha.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\|A\|_1
=
\alpha
=
\max_{1\leq j\leq n}
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ij}|.
$$
